summary: Gap-closing wave: verify & enrich the Swiss/local threads surfaced from the /data corpus (FINMA risk classification, SBB/KPMG/BNP, Swiss adoption stats, EU AI Act 2026 delay, big-tech %-of-code claims, latest benchmarks) with fresh web searches

result.thread: FINMA classified an advanced AI cyber capability ("Mythos-class") as an "immediate systemic risk" around May 2026; FINMA expects centralized AI inventory, model-risk management, board accountability; a 2nd-gen FINMA AI circular is expected to crystallize by end-2026.
result.verified: MOSTLY CONFIRMED with two corrections. (1) The "Mythos systemic risk" core is CONFIRMED and citable to public, independent sources. A FINMA spokesperson told Bloomberg (24 Apr 2026, also carried verbatim by swissinfo.ch) that "the uncontrolled and immediate availability of AI models such as Mythos would be classified as a systemic risk." Mythos is a real, named Anthropic model (controlled rollout "Project Glasswing", ~40 vetted parties) that autonomously finds/exploits zero-day vulnerabilities across major OSes and browsers. FINMA warned "virtually all existing software systems could simultaneously be affected by a multitude of previously unknown zero-day vulnerabilities, which would be exploited immediately and via AI." The IMF independently called for regulators to treat AI models like Mythos as a systemic risk (IMF blog, 7 May 2026), and the US Treasury/Fed convened bank CEOs over the same model (Apr 2026). CORRECTION on wording/date: the public phrase is "would be classified as a systemic risk" (conditional, about uncontrolled/immediate AVAILABILITY of the model to the market), NOT FINMA formally "classifying Mythos-class as an immediate systemic risk." The dateline is 24 Apr 2026, not "around May 2026" (the May 2026 date matches the IMF's separate systemic-risk call). "Mythos-class" is corpus shorthand, not FINMA terminology. (2) The governance expectations are CONFIRMED: FINMA Guidance 08/2024 (18 Dec 2024) and the Apr 2025 FINMA AI survey establish that supervised institutions must maintain an inventory/overview of AI applications, manage model risk (robustness, correctness, explainability, bias), assign clear board/senior-management responsibility and accountability (avoiding decentralized ownership), and apply outsourcing/third-party due-diligence rules to bought-in AI. (3) CANNOT CONFIRM the specific "2nd-gen FINMA AI circular crystallizing by end-2026" timeline. Public sources show only that FINMA "announced its intention to refine its expectations ... and, where necessary, to make them transparent in the market by issuing further guidance notes or circulars" — no public end-2026 deadline exists. Note Guidance 08/2024 is non-binding ("supervisory expectations," not a Rundschreiben); a binding AI circular remains a possibility FINMA has flagged, not a scheduled deliverable. Treat the end-2026 timeline as internal/speculative signal.

enriched_findings.claim: FINMA stated that uncontrolled, immediate market availability of Anthropic's Mythos AI model would be classified as a systemic risk to the Swiss financial system; it warned virtually all software could be hit simultaneously by previously unknown zero-day vulnerabilities exploited immediately via AI.
enriched_findings.evidence: FINMA spokesperson to Bloomberg, carried verbatim by SWI swissinfo.ch (Swiss public broadcaster, independent of FINMA): 'The uncontrolled and immediate availability of AI models such as Mythos would be classified as a systemic risk.' Article also reports FINMA expects banks to 'actively incorporate the evolving threat landscape into their risk management' with 'strong awareness of the risks at all levels, continuous communication with service providers, and a clearly risk-oriented approach.' [Independent media, FINMA-sourced quote]

enriched_findings.claim: The IMF independently framed AI models such as Mythos as a systemic (not merely operational) financial-stability risk and urged regulators to respond with cyber stress testing, board-level oversight, tighter third-party/cloud oversight, and containment controls.

[Independent media + IMF primary]

enriched_findings.claim: FINMA Guidance 08/2024 sets out supervisory expectations for AI: governance with clear responsibility/accountability, an inventory/overview of AI applications, model-risk management (robustness, correctness, explainability, bias), data quality, ongoing monitoring/documentation, and compliance with outsourcing rules for third-party AI.

[Regulator primary]

enriched_findings.claim: Independent legal commentary confirms FINMA's four areas (data quality, explainability/transparency, risk identification & assessment, governance) and that the guidance requires central management/accountability, ongoing risk-identification mechanisms (performance indicators, data-quality tests, stability), and adherence to regulatory outsourcing requirements for third-party AI.

enriched_findings.evidence: Multiple independent legal sources (e.g. Pestalozzi, VISCHER) and FINMA's own documentation note FINMA 'announced its intention to refine its expectations ... and, where necessary, to make them transparent in the market by issuing further guidance notes or circulars' — conditional, with no published 2026 deadline. The end-2026 crystallization date appears to be an internal/speculative inference, not a publicly documented FINMA commitment. [Independent legal commentary + regulator dossier]

result.caveats: For the CIO pitch, present three tiers of confidence. STRONG/CITABLE: (a) FINMA Guidance 08/2024 governance expectations — AI inventory, model-risk management, board accountability, third-party/outsourcing due diligence — are real, public, and exactly the controls the pitch should promise to satisfy (FINMA primary + independent legal commentary). (b) The Apr 2025 FINMA survey (~50% adoption, governance lagging) and Nov 2025 Risk Monitor (cyber + third-party concentration as systemic concerns) are solid public anchors. (c) The Mythos systemic-risk statement is real and independently corroborated (FINMA spokesperson via Bloomberg/swissinfo, IMF, US Treasury/Fed) — a powerful "AI is now a board-level systemic-risk topic" hook. TWO CORRECTIONS to make before pitching: (1) Precise wording is "uncontrolled and immediate AVAILABILITY of AI models such as Mythos would be classified as a systemic risk" — it is a conditional statement about market availability of an offensive-cyber model, NOT FINMA formally classifying a "Mythos-class capability" as an "immediate systemic risk." The date is 24 Apr 2026, not May 2026. Do not over-claim. (2) The "2nd-gen FINMA AI circular by end-2026" is NOT publicly documented — FINMA has only said it MAY issue further guidance notes or circulars. Frame as "FINMA has signalled it may move from non-binding guidance toward a binding circular," not as a confirmed end-2026 deadline. SOURCING FLAGS: FINMA.ch = regulator primary; swissinfo.ch, Bloomberg, American Banker, IMF, Sullivan & Cromwell = independent; MLL/Pestalozzi/VISCHER = independent legal commentary. Bloomberg URL is paywalled (403) — cite swissinfo.ch as the accessible equivalent carrying the same FINMA quote. The IMF primary blog returned 403 on direct fetch but is corroborated via American Banker; cite both.

result.thread: SBB went live with a 30,000-employee multilingual RAG assistant (Mistral/SAP); KPMG deployed Claude across 138 countries / 276,000 staff; BNP Paribas extended a 3-year Mistral partnership citing sovereign-AI/defense rationale; Swiss survey: ~88% of firms use AI but ~41% report no ROI; ~73% of Swiss internet users have tried GenAI.
result.verified: Five sub-claims, four CONFIRMED and one PARTIALLY CORRECTED. (1) SBB Mistral/SAP RAG assistant: CONFIRMED by a vendor primary source (Mistral AI customer page, dated 2026-04-24). The multilingual (DE/FR/IT) chatbot runs on Mistral Large via SAP-operated EU infrastructure (RAG over FAQs/training/screenshots, glossary query-rewriting, human-in-the-loop), scaled from a 1,000-user pilot to 30,000 employees, with an estimated ~80% reduction in repetitive support queries. Numbers match the corpus exactly. Caveat: it is a vendor case study tied to SBB's SAP S/4HANA migration (internal IT support), not a customer-facing or coding tool, and SBB has not issued its own public press release on it. (2) KPMG-Anthropic: CONFIRMED by primary sources on BOTH sides (Anthropic newsroom + KPMG press release, both 2026-05-19/20). 276,000+ staff across 138 countries/territories; Claude (Cowork + Managed Agents) embedded in KPMG's Digital Gateway on Microsoft Azure; expands a ~2-year US pilot; Anthropic also names KPMG a preferred private-equity partner. Independently covered by Fortune, TNW. Exact match. (3) BNP Paribas-Mistral: CONFIRMED (Bloomberg 2026-02-11 + BNP Paribas own press release; Retail Banker International). A 3-year extension building on a 2023 collaboration formalized into a group-wide deal in 2024; scope spans CIB, CPBS, KYC, co-development and a 2026 GenAI employee-assistant rollout. The 'sovereign-AI' framing is CONFIRMED in substance (BNP explicitly cites choosing a European technology partner as part of a multi-model approach guided by data sensitivity and geographic considerations); however the specific 'defense' rationale is NOT in the deal text — it comes from later May-2026 trade coverage linking Mistral's new cyber/defense-oriented model to the partnership, so 'defense rationale' is editorial color, not a BNP statement. (4) '~88% use AI / ~41% no ROI': PARTIALLY CORRECTED / CANNOT CONFIRM as a single Swiss study. No Swiss survey states this pair. The 88% is the GLOBAL McKinsey 'State of AI' figure (88% of orgs use AI in at least one function), not Swiss. Swiss-specific 2026 data is LOWER and differently framed: the UBS/Intervista study (2026-05-20, ~2,500 Swiss firms) found ~60% use AI tools and roughly one-third use none; Deloitte Switzerland's AI ROI report (Aug-Sep 2025, 99 Swiss respondents) frames it as only ~1 in 3 having turned experimentation into financial gains. The '41% no ROI' most likely echoes either the global MIT NANDA 'GenAI Divide' study (95% of GenAI pilots deliver little/no measurable ROI, Aug 2025) or Deloitte's 'only ~1/3 see returns' finding — not a clean Swiss 41%. Recommend the pitch use the precise Swiss/Deloitte/MIT figures rather than the conflated 88%/41%. (5) '~73% of Swiss internet users tried GenAI': CONFIRMED by an independent academic primary source — University of Zurich WIP-CH 2025 study (survey run by gfs.bern, 1,078 internet users 14+, June-Aug 2025): adoption rose 37% (2023) to 54% (2024) to 73% (2025); 47% use it at least monthly, 84% among 14-19s. Exact match.

result.thread: EU AI Act "Digital Omnibus" deal (~May 2026): deferred high-risk Annex III obligations to ~Dec 2027 and Annex I to ~Aug 2028; sandboxes to Aug 2027; and the claim that agentic CODING tools are generally NOT "high-risk" under the Act.
result.verified:
CONFIRMED on all four sub-claims, with two precision points the CIO deck should reflect.

1) DATES — CONFIRMED EXACTLY. The Digital Omnibus on AI defers standalone high-risk Annex III obligations from 2 Aug 2026 to 2 December 2027, and product-embedded Annex I high-risk obligations from 2 Aug 2027 to 2 August 2028. Regulatory sandboxes move to 2 August 2027. These figures are consistent across the EU Council (Consilium) press release, the European Parliament Legislative Train, and 8+ independent law firms (Gibson Dunn, White & Case, Hogan Lovells, DLA Piper, Travers Smith, CMS, Mishcon, Covington/Inside Privacy). The corpus's "~Dec 2027 / ~Aug 2028 / Aug 2027" is precise.

2) LEGAL STATUS — IMPORTANT CORRECTION OF STATUS, NOT DATES. As of June 2026 this is NOT yet enacted law. It is a provisional political (trilogue) agreement reached 7 May 2026, approved by member-state ambassadors (Coreper) on 13 May 2026, and "close to adoption" per the European Parliament. Formal Parliament/Council adoption and Official Journal publication are expected June–July 2026, before the 2 Aug 2026 trigger. The new dates do NOT legally bind until OJ publication. So for the CIO: the relief is essentially certain but technically not yet final at pitch time — frame as "agreed and pending formal adoption," not "in force."

3) CORPUS'S "Aug 2026 high-risk lands" ASSUMPTION — CORRECTLY OVERTURNED. The original AI Act would have applied standalone high-risk obligations on 2 Aug 2026; the Omnibus pushes that to 2 Dec 2027. The earlier internal assumption (high-risk lands Aug 2026) is superseded. Nuance worth a footnote: the obligations are also tied to readiness of harmonised standards/support tools, with 2 Dec 2027 / 2 Aug 2028 as the long-stop backstop dates.

4) GPAI / Code of Practice — CONFIRMED UNCHANGED. GPAI model obligations have applied since 2 Aug 2025 and are NOT delayed by the Omnibus; the EU AI Office's GPAI enforcement powers (fines, model recalls) still switch on 2 Aug 2026. The (voluntary) GPAI Code of Practice still stands. Relevant because the LLMs powering coding agents are GPAI — that layer's obligations sit with the model provider (e.g. Anthropic/OpenAI/etc.), not the bank as a deployer.

5) AGENTIC CODING TOOLS NOT HIGH-RISK — CONFIRMED (caveated). An AI assistant for writing/reviewing/refactoring/debugging code does not, on its face, fall into any of the eight Annex III high-risk domains, and code generation is not a regulated safety component under Annex I/Article 6. So a coding copilot used for normal SDLC is generally not high-risk. CAVEAT the deck must keep: classification turns on USE, not the tool. It flips to high-risk if the bank wires coding/IDE telemetry into worker-evaluation, productivity-ranking, promotion/retention or PR-routing-by-developer-history (Annex III point 4 — employment/worker management), or if AI-generated code is embedded into a regulated safety-critical product. Governance ask: keep agentic coding scoped to the dev workflow and out of HR/worker-monitoring uses. Note: the most coding-specific source (Augment Code) is a VENDOR; the underlying Annex III/Article 6 reasoning is independently grounded in the AI Act text (artificialintelligenceact.eu) and law-firm analysis.

VENDOR source; the Article 6 / Annex III legal basis is independently confirmed by artificialintelligenceact.eu and law-firm analysis.

enriched_findings.claim: A coding tool CAN become high-risk depending on use — chiefly if its output/telemetry is wired into worker evaluation, monitoring, productivity ranking, or HR decisions (Annex III point 4, employment), or if AI code is embedded into a regulated safety-critical product. Classification turns on use, not the tool.
enriched_findings.evidence: Augment Code / Article 6 analysis: teams 'reach high-risk classification by wiring Copilot or GitHub telemetry into a manager-facing productivity dashboard,' or by 'using AI output to influence retention, promotion, or task assignment decisions' — 'the regulation reaches AI used about or affecting workers.' Independent legal reasoning grounds this in Annex III point 4 (employment/worker management) and Article 6 classification rules. (Coding-specific framing is VENDOR; Annex III legal basis is independent.)

2) Switzerland is not in the EU. Raiffeisen Schweiz is a Swiss bank; the EU AI Act applies extraterritorially only where outputs/systems are placed on or used in the EU market (e.g. EU customers, EU subsidiaries, or providers placing systems on the EU market). For a purely-Swiss-domestic developer-tooling use case the AI Act may not directly apply at all — the relevant Swiss regime (FINMA guidance / planned Swiss AI regulation aligned to the Council of Europe AI Convention) is the primary lens.
